Appendix D Symmetries

The original algorithm proposed to account for symmetry in Ref. [22] was based on the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization of the symmetry generators. This algorithm is suited for systems with a reduced number of atoms in the unit cell, but scales as na6n_{a}^{6}, with nan_{a} the number of atoms in the unit cell. This symmetrization procedure becomes thus a real bottleneck of the SSCHA code for systems with more than 30 atoms in the unit cell. In the version of the code we describe here, the orthonormalized generators are not calculated and, instead, the starting dynamical matrix and the gradient are directly symmetrized. The symmetrization of the dynamical matrix, or its gradient, is made in 𝐪\mathbf{q} space, which allows for a very fast implementation even for big supercells.

The code enforces all the symmetries in the auxiliary force constant matrix as

𝚽⁡(𝐪)=1NS​∑i=1NS𝐓S^i​(Si−1​𝐪)​𝚽​(Si−1​𝐪)​𝐓S^i†​(Si−1​𝐪),\bm{\varPhi}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\mathbf{T}_{\hat{S}_{i}}(S_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{q})\bm{\varPhi}(S_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{q})\mathbf{T}_{\hat{S}_{i}}^{\dagger}(S_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{q}), (112)

where SiS_{i} are the 3×\times3 point group matrices of the space group, NSN_{S} the number of symmetries of the crystal, 𝐓S^​(𝐪)\mathbf{T}_{\hat{S}}(\mathbf{q}) are unitary matrices that represent the SS symmetry in the 𝐪\mathbf{q} point. These matrices are reported in Refs. [87, 88, 89]. To find the symmetries given the structure, we wrapped into the SSCHA the symmetry module of Quantum ESPRESSO[63, 64].

This operation is performed also on the gradient of the dynamical matrix each time it is computed. Since the dynamical matrices satisfying the symmetries define a linear subspace, if both the gradient and the original dynamical matrix belong to this subspace, any linear combination of them will also satisfy the symmetry constrains. Thus, it is necessary to symmetrize the dynamical matrix once at the beginning, and then apply the symmetry constrains only to the gradient to preserve the symmetries in the whole simulation.

The symmetry module from Quantum ESPRESSO only recognizes symmetries when the unit cell is the primitive one. Sometimes, it could be convenient to choose a different unit cell. Therefore, we also interfaced the SSCHA code with the spglib package[90] to improve the identification of symmetries. Instead of working in the unit cell in 𝐪\mathbf{q} space, spglib provides the symmetry operations in real space. In this case, the SSCHA code divides the symmetry matrices identified by spglib into pure translations and point group operations. Then, symmetries are enforced in real space by first imposing pure translations, followed by point group operations as

𝚽=1NS​∑i=1NS𝐓S^i​𝚽​𝐓S^i†.\bm{\varPhi}=\frac{1}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\mathbf{T}_{\hat{S}_{i}}\bm{\varPhi}\mathbf{T}_{\hat{S}_{i}}^{\dagger}. (113)

Then, the permutation symmetry on the indices is imposed. Finally, the code transforms back the real space dynamical matrix (or the gradient) in 𝐪\mathbf{q} space.

This operation takes more time than the symmetrization in 𝐪\mathbf{q} space, as it is performed in the supercell. However, due to its simplicity and to avoid the cumbersome 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space symmetrization of higher-order force constants, the same supercell approach is used to symmetrize the third- and fourth-order force constant matrices, namely Φ(3)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(3)}}}{\Phi} and Φ(4)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(4)}}}{\Phi} introduced in Sec. III.2.

Symmetries are also enforced on the average positions of the nuclei (and the forces). After computing the SCHA forces on atom tt along direction α\alpha, ftα\text{f}^{\alpha}_{t}, we impose symmetry as

ftα=1NS​∑i=1NS∑t=1na∑β=13Siα​β​fS−1​(t)β,\text{f}_{t}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\sum_{t=1}^{n_{a}}\sum_{\beta=1}^{3}{S_{i}}_{\alpha\beta}\text{f}_{S^{-1}(t)}^{\beta}, (114)

where S−1​(t)S^{-1}(t) is the atom in which the SS symmetry maps the tt one to. In this way, the forces are correctly directed only along the Wyckoff coordinates, and the atomic positions relax subsequently keeping the correct Wyckoff positions.

D.1 Acoustic sum rule on the auxiliary force constants

Besides space group symmetries, also the acoustic sum rule (ASR) must be imposed. The acoustic sum rule is a condition that arises from the momentum conservation (the center of mass of the system is fixed). The energy must not change after a rigid translation of the whole system. This can be translated in a trivial condition for the force constant matrix in the supercell:

∑tΦs​tα​β=∑sΦs​tα​β=0.\sum_{t}\varPhi_{st}^{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{s}\varPhi_{st}^{\alpha\beta}=0. (115)

In general, the SSCHA gradient computed from a finite ensemble violates this condition due to the stochastic noise. We enforce the sum rule on the gradient at each step. As for the symmetries, also matrices that satisfy the acoustic sum rule define a linear subspace. Thus we define the orthogonal projector operator that enforces the acoustic sum rule as

𝚽(a​s​r)=𝑷​𝚽​𝑷†.\bm{\varPhi}^{(asr)}={\bm{P}}\bm{\varPhi}{\bm{P}}^{\dagger}. (116)

The projection matrix in real space is

Ps​tα​β=δs​t​δα​β−δα​βna​∑u=1naδt​u.P_{st}^{\alpha\beta}=\delta_{st}\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\frac{\delta_{\alpha\beta}}{n_{a}}\sum_{u=1}^{n_{a}}\delta_{tu}. (117)

This operation only affects the dynamical matrix at Γ\Gamma. The same projector is employed to impose the ASR on the forces:

f(a​s​r)sα=(𝑷​f)sα=fsα−1na​∑k=1nafkα{\text{f}^{(asr)}}_{s}^{\alpha}=({\bm{P}}f)_{s}^{\alpha}=\text{f}_{s}^{\alpha}-\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{k=1}^{n_{a}}\text{f}_{k}^{\alpha} (118)

Notably, it can be proved that this procedure does not spoil the symmetrization described above.

This ASR imposition procedure analytically cancels out the frequencies of acoustic modes at Γ\Gamma and any rigid translation of the atomic positions, thus it is the most indicated for the SSCHA minimization. A different approach, implemented for the Fourier interpolation, is described in Appendix E.2. The latter affects not just phonons at Γ\Gamma, and, thus, it is more suited for interpolating dynamical matrices close to the Brillouin zone center.

Appendix E Reciprocal space formalism and Fourier interpolation

E.1 Reciprocal space formalism

The SSCHA code is designed to be used with crystals, thus it takes advantage of lattice periodicity and Fourier transforms the relevant quantities with respect to the lattice vectors. That allows to make independent analysis for each 𝒒\bm{q} point in reciprocal space. When we need to stress this aspect, we will modify the notation adopted, partitioning the supercell atomic index into a unit-cell index plus a lattice index (s,𝒍)(s,\bm{l}), with ss now ranging from 1 to nan_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{a}}} (the number of atoms in the unit cell), and 𝒍\bm{l} being a 3 dimensional integer vector assuming NcN_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{c}}} total values (the numer of unit cells forming the supercell). Thus, in this notation, in general we will have nn-th order tensors in a 3​na3n_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{a}}} dimensional space (indicated with bold symbols, in free-component notation), which in real space depend on nn lattice-vector parameters, 𝑫(n)​(𝒍1,…​𝒍n)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{(n)}}{\bm{D}}(\bm{l}_{1},\ldots\bm{l}_{n}) (to be precise, due to the translation symmetry, this real-space tensor actually depends only on n−1n-1 independent values 𝒍i\bm{l}_{i}). The reciprocal-space expression of such a tensor, 𝑫(n)​(𝒒1,…,𝒒n)\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{(n)}}{\bm{D}}(\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}), is obtained through the Fourier transform

𝑫(n)​(𝒒1,…,𝒒n)=1Nc​∑𝒍1​…​𝒍nei​∑h𝒒h⋅𝒍h​𝑫(n)​(𝒍1,…,𝒍n).\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{(n)}}{\bm{D}}(\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n})=\frac{1}{N_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{c}}}}\sum_{\bm{l}_{1}\ldots\bm{l}_{n}}e^{i\sum_{h}\bm{q}_{h}\cdot\bm{l}_{h}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{(n)}}{\bm{D}}(\bm{l}_{1},\ldots,\bm{l}_{n}). (119)

Notice that, due to the lattice translation symmetry, 𝑫(S)​(𝒒1,…,𝒒n){\bm{D}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}(\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}) is zero unless ∑h𝒒h\sum_{h}\bm{q}_{h} is a reciprocal lattice vector, thus we have again only n−1n-1 independent parameters 𝒒i\bm{q}_{i}. In particular, after the calculation performed on a real-space supercell, for each 𝒒\bm{q} point of the commensurate grid of the reciprocal-space unit cell, the SSCHA code computes the Fourier transformed matrices 𝑫(S)​(−𝒒,𝒒){\bm{D}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}(-\bm{q},\bm{q}), which we will shortly indicate as 𝑫(S)​(𝒒){\bm{D}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}(\bm{q}), and the relative eigenvalues ωμ​(𝒒)\omega_{\mu}(\bm{q}) and eigenvectors 𝒆μ​(𝒒)\bm{e}_{\mu}(\bm{q}). Similarly, the Hessian calculation provides the matrix 𝑫(F)​(−𝒒,𝒒)\bm{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(F)}}}(-\bm{q},\bm{q}), which we indicate as 𝑫(F)​(𝒒)\bm{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(F)}}}(\bm{q}), where (see Eq. (61))

𝑫(F)​(𝒒)=𝑫(S)​(𝒒)+𝚷⁡(𝒒,0),\bm{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(F)}}}(\bm{q})={\bm{D}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}(\bm{q})+\bm{\Pi}(\bm{q},0)\,, (120)

and its eigenvalues Ωμ​(𝒒)\Omega_{\mu}(\bm{q}) and eigenvectors 𝒇μ​(𝒒)\bm{f}_{\mu}(\bm{q}).

E.2 Fourier interpolation: centering and acoustic sum rule

The SSCHA code computes the FCs in real space supercells with periodic boundary conditions (PBCs). As shown in the previous section, a crucial feature of the SSCHA code is the use of the Fourier interpolation technique in order to extrapolate the results to the thermodynamic limit (infinite supercell results) without recurring to expensive large supercell calculations. In order to Fourier interpolate the computed FCs on arbitrary points of the reciprocal space, as a first thing it is necessary to reconstruct the real-space infinite-crystal FCs from them. Roughly speaking, this is done by removing the PBCs, i.e. superlattice equivalent atoms are not considered identical anymore, and assuming that only the FCs between atoms in the same supercell are different from zero. Of course, this gives correct results as long as the supercell used in the calculations is large enough to consider negligible the FCs between atoms at distances comparable with the distances between the periodic boundary replica. However, an intrinsic arbtrariness is present in this recipe, due to the fact that the supercell is not univocally defined and the choice of different supercells leads to different interpolation results (i.e. as long as the reciprocal-space point in which we are interpolating does not belong to the original commensurate grid, different - yet superlattice equivalent - lattice points give different contributions to the Fourier transform). This problem is solved by wisely selecting the supercell according to a prescription based on a physical principle: among equivalent superlattice points, the ones closest to each other must be selected. This procedure defines the so called “centering” of the FCs and, as explained, it is a necessary step to be done before Fourier interpolating the real space FCs. The SSCHA code centers 2nd and 3rd order FCs (with a procedure that can be generalized to any nnth-order FCs. In particular, the next release of the code will apply the same procedure to center and interpolate the 4th order FCs). Here we explictly describe the 3rd FCs centering algorithm [91].

The PBCs are defined on a superlattice ℛlat(S)\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}} of the original lattice ℛlat\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}. The lattice vectors set ℛlat\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}} can be equivalently described as the superlattice ℛlat(S)\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}} plus the basis given by the lattice vectors in a superlattice unit cell S​CSC. In other words, a lattice vector 𝒍∈ℛlat\bm{l}\in\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}} indentifies a set of superlattice-equivalent lattice vectors {𝒍+𝑻 with 𝑻∈ℛlat(S)}\{\bm{l}+\bm{T}\,\,\text{ with }\bm{T}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}\}, and we have ℛlat={𝒍+𝑻 with 𝒍∈SC,𝑻∈ℛlat(S)}\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}=\{\bm{l}+\bm{T}\,\,\text{ with }\bm{l}\in SC\,,\bm{T}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}\}. Given three atoms s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3} in the unit cells 𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}, respectively (due to the lattice translation symmetry we can confine the first atom to the origin unit cell), they indentify a triangle with vertices in 𝝉s1,𝝉s2+𝒍2,𝝉s3+𝒍3\bm{\tau}_{s_{1}},\bm{\tau}_{s_{2}}+\bm{l}_{2},\bm{\tau}_{s_{3}}+\bm{l}_{3} (𝝉si\bm{\tau}_{s_{i}} is the position vector of atom sis_{i} in the original unit cell). For these three points we define the weight 𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) in this way: it is zero if there is at least another “equivalent-vertices” triangle having as vertices points 𝝉s1\bm{\tau}_{s_{1}}, 𝝉s2+𝒍2+𝑻2\bm{\tau}_{s_{2}}+\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2}, 𝝉s3+𝒍3+𝑻3\bm{\tau}_{s_{3}}+\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3} with 𝑻2,𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)\bm{T}_{2},\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}} (i.e. points that are superlattice-equivalent to 𝝉s1,𝝉s2+𝒍2,𝝉s3+𝒍3\bm{\tau}_{s_{1}},\bm{\tau}_{s_{2}}+\bm{l}_{2},\bm{\tau}_{s_{3}}+\bm{l}_{3}) with smaller perimeter, otherwise it is the inverse of the number of equivalent-vertices triangles having the same (minimal) perimeter. In formulas, indicated with 𝒫s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2+𝑻2,𝒍3+𝑻3)\mathcal{P}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3}) the perimeter of the triangle with vertices 𝝉s1\bm{\tau}_{s_{1}}, 𝝉s2+𝒍2+𝑻2\bm{\tau}_{s_{2}}+\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2}, 𝝉s3+𝒍3+𝑻3\bm{\tau}_{s_{3}}+\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3}, this amounts to

W_s_1s_2s_3(0,l_2,l_3)= { 0 [ [ if ∃ T 2 ,T 3 ∈R (S) lat : P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 +T 2 ,l 3 +T 3 ) ¡ P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 ,l 3 ) [ # (T 2 ,T 3 )∈R (S) lat : P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 +T 2 ,l 3 +T 3 ) = P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 ,l 3 ) ] -1 [ [ if ∄ T 2 ,T 3 ∈R (S) lat : P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 +T 2 ,l 3 +T 3 ) ¡ P s 1 s 2 s 3 (0,l 2 ,l 3 ) (121)

The weights 𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) are pure geometrical factors, different from zero for “compact” three-atom clusters, and they satisfy the normalization

∑𝑻2,𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2+𝑻2,𝒍3+𝑻3)=1∀𝒍2,𝒍3∈ℛlat∀s1,s2,s3∈{1,…,na}.\sum_{\bm{T}_{2},\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3})=1\mkern 80.0mu\begin{aligned} &\forall\,\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}\\ &\forall\,s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}\in\{1,\ldots,n_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{a}}}\}\,.\end{aligned} (122)

The weights are used to define the centering. Given a 3rd-order FCs, Φs1,s2,s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}), its “centered” version Φ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) is given by

Φ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3=Φ(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3×𝒲s1​s2​s3(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3),\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})=\Phi{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\,\times\,\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\,, (123)

where we have separately indicated cartesian (αh\alpha_{h}) and atomic (shs_{h}) indices. The idea behind this definition is pretty simple: once the PBCs are discarded, of the infinite set of superlattice-equivalent atoms only the“closest one” are characterized by a force constant different from zero. If there are several equivalent triplets at the minimal reciprocal distance, all of them are considered (to preserve the symmetry) and the force constants are consequently scaled (to avoid a wrong multiple counting effect). The centering definition has some degree of arbitrariness, though, due to the arbitrariness of the criterion employed to evaluate the “size” of a three atoms cluster. We took the perimeter of the triangle, a criterion that is a direct generalization of the distance between atoms, which is the one used in the 2nd order FCs centering. More in general, for an nn-atoms cluster this size measure is readily generalized as the sum of the distances between all the n⁡(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2 couples of atoms. However, even if in principle other choices could be done, this arbitrariness is immaterial as long as the supercell calculation is large enough (in the thermodynamic limit all the possible choices, if reasonable, are expected to be equivalent).

A delicate issue is associated with the centering: the spoiling of the acoustic sum rule (ASR). For a nnth-order FC, the acoustic sum rule is

∑𝒍i∑siΦs1​…​si​…​snα1​…​αi​…​αn​(𝒍1,…,𝒍i,…,𝒍n)=0​∀αh∈{x,y,z}∀sh∈{1​…​na} with ​h≠i∀𝒍h∈ℛlat with ​h≠i.\sum_{\bm{l}_{i}}\sum_{s_{i}}\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{i}\ldots\alpha_{n}}_{s_{1}\ldots s_{i}\ldots s_{n}}(\bm{l}_{1},\ldots,\bm{l}_{i},\ldots,\bm{l}_{n})=0\begin{aligned} &\mkern 40.0mu\forall\,\alpha_{h}\in\{x,y,z\}&&\\ &\mkern 40.0mu\forall\,s_{h}\in\{1\ldots n_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{a}}}\}&&\text{ with }h\neq i\\ &\mkern 40.0mu\forall\,\bm{l}_{h}\in\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}&&\text{ with }h\neq i\end{aligned}\quad. (124)

The ASR comes is crucial, among other things, to have the correct acoustic phonon dispersion at and close to Γ\Gamma. The FCs computed with SSCHA (in supercells with PBCs) fulfill the acoustic sum rule but, in general, the centering spoils it (except for the n=2n=2 case). In fact, in general the centered FCs fulfill a “weaker” version of the ASR in Eq. (124), since only the simultaneous sum on n−1n-1 indices is zero:

∑𝒍i1,…,𝒍in−1∑si1,…,sin−1Φ(cent)(𝒍1,…,𝒍n)s1​…​snα1​…​αn=0.\sum_{\bm{l}_{i_{1}},\ldots,\bm{l}_{i_{n-1}}}\sum_{s_{i_{1}},\ldots,s_{i_{n-1}}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{n}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}\ldots s_{n}}(\bm{l}_{1},\ldots,\bm{l}_{n})=0\,. (125)

In particular, this explains why the centering of 2nd-order FCs does not spoil the ASR (for n=2n=2 the weak ASR is nothing but the proper ASR, as the sum over n−1n-1 indices coincides with the sum over one index).

In order to see why this happens let us consider, as an example, the 3rd-order FCs case and the sum over the third index. It is:

∑s3∑𝒍3∈ℛlatΦ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3=\displaystyle\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\,{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})= (126)
=∑s3∑𝒍3∈S​C∑𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)Φ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3+𝑻3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\sum_{\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3}) (127)
=∑s3∑𝒍3∈S​C∑𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3+𝑻3)​𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3+𝑻3)\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\sum_{\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3})\,\,\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3}) (128)
=∑s3∑𝒍3∈S​C∑𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)​𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3+𝑻3)\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\sum_{\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\,\,\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3}) (129)
=∑s3∑𝒍3∈S​CΦs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)​∑𝑻3∈ℛlat(S)𝒲s1​s2​s3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3+𝑻3)⏟nonconstant w.r.t. ​s3​ and ​𝒍3.\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\,\,\underbrace{\sum_{\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3})}_{\text{nonconstant w.r.t. }s_{3}\text{ and }\bm{l}_{3}}\,. (130)

Since the last factor, highlighted with a brace under, in general is not constant with respect to s3s_{3} and 𝒍3\bm{l}_{3}, it cannot be factored out from the sums, so that the ASR for the original Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})

∑s3∑𝒍3∈S​CΦs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)=0\sum_{s_{3}}\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})=0 (131)

cannot be used to obtain the ASR for the centered Φ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}). However, using Eq. (122), with similar passages we can show that the sum over the last two indices is zero:

∑s2,s3∑𝒍2,𝒍3∈ℛlatΦ(cent)(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3=\displaystyle\sum_{s_{2},s_{3}}\,\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\,{\overset{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(cent)}}}{\Phi}}{}^{\mkern-8.0mu\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{\mkern-8.0mus_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})=\vphantom{\underbrace{\sum_{\bm{T}_{2}\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3})}_{=1}} (132)

=∑s2,s3∑𝒍2,𝒍3∈S​CΦs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=\sum_{s_{2},s_{3}}\,\,\sum_{\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}\in SC}\,\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\vphantom{\underbrace{\sum_{\bm{T}_{2}\bm{T}_{3}\in\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(S)}}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{lat}}}}\mathcal{W}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2}+\bm{T}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}+\bm{T}_{3})}_{=1}} (134)
=0,\displaystyle\mkern 80.0mu=0\,, (135)

thus the weak ASR is fulfilled.

The spoling of the ASR after the centering dictates to impose it. In principle, there is not a unique way of doing it, as imposing the ASR on FCs simply consists in finding new FCs that fullfil the ASR and differ the least from the original FCs (according to some reasonable but arbitrary metric). In this release of the SSCHA code we impose the ASR by employing an iterative procedure, consisting of two steps [91]. First, the ASR is imposed on one index (the last one, for example). This spoils the permutation symmetry, which is consequently imposed. In general, the resulting permutation-symmetric FCs do not fulfill the ASR yet, thus this procedure is repeatedly applied until the permutation-symmetric FCs fulfill the ASR within a certain tolerance. The imposition of the permutation symmetry is a straightforward task. The ASR is imposed on the third index of a centered 3rd-order FCs by updating its values on the compact three-atom clusters that defined the centering (in order to preserve the short-sightdness of the centered FCs even after the ASR imposition). Given a centered Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}), the Φ~(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3\widetilde{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) that fulfills the ASR on the third index is computed with

Φ~(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3=Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)−𝒦s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3|p)×∑s¯3,𝒍¯3Φs1​s2​s¯3α1​α2​α3(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍¯3),\widetilde{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})=\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})-\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}|p)\times\sum_{\overline{s}_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})\,, (136)

where 𝒦s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3|p)\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}|p) is the scaling factor

𝒦s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3|p)={|Φs1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)|p∑s¯3,𝒍¯3|Φs1​s2​s¯3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍¯3)|pif p=0orp>0​ and ​∑s¯3,𝒍¯3|Φs1​s2​s¯3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍¯3)|≠00if p>0​ and ​∑s¯3,𝒍¯3|Φs1​s2​s¯3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍¯3)|=0,\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}|p)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\left|\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3})\right|^{p}}{\sum_{\overline{s}_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\left|\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})\right|^{p}}&&\text{if }\mkern 20.0mu&&p=0\mkern 40.0mu\text{or}\mkern 40.0mup>0\mkern 10.0mu\text{ and }\mkern 10.0mu\sum_{\overline{s}_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\left|\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})\right|\neq 0\\ &\mkern 90.0mu0\vphantom{\frac{\sum_{\overline{s}_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})}{\sum_{s_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\left|\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})\right|^{p}}}&&\text{if }\mkern 20.0mu&&p>0\mkern 10.0mu\text{ and }\mkern 10.0mu\sum_{\overline{s}_{3},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3}}\left|\Phi^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}\overline{s}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\overline{\bm{l}}_{3})\right|=0\end{aligned}\right.\,, (137)

with pp a non-negative real number which can be arbitrarily fixed to optimize the calculation performances (in the equation above the convention 00=10^{0}=1 has been adopted). The Φ~(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3\widetilde{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) defined through Eq. (136) fulfills the ASR on the third index, since for any p≥0p\geq 0 the scaling factor fulfills the normalization condition

∑s3,𝒍3𝒦s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3|p)=1.\sum_{s_{3},\bm{l}_{3}}\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}|p)=1\,. (138)

The value of pp has effects on the way the different terms of Φ(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3)s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}) are scaled. For p=0p=0 the scaling factor is a pure geometric quantity related to the three atoms clusters. Indeed, given s1,s2,𝒍2s_{1},s_{2},\bm{l}_{2}, the scaling factor 𝒦s1​s2​s3α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3|p=0)\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}_{3}|p=0) is fully determined (it is the same for all the αh,s3,𝒍3\alpha_{h},s_{3},\bm{l}_{3}) and, in particular, it does not depend on the FCs value. On the contrary, for p≠0p\neq 0, given αh,s1,s2,𝒍2\alpha_{h},s_{1},s_{2},\bm{l}_{2} we have

𝒦s1​s2​s3′α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3′|p)𝒦s1​s2​s3′′α1​α2​α3​(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍3′′|p)=|Φα1​α2​α3s1​s2​s3′′(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍′′3)Φα1​α2​α3s1​s2​s3′(𝟎,𝒍2,𝒍′3)|p\frac{\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s^{\prime}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}^{\prime}_{3}|p)}{\mathcal{K}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s^{\prime\prime}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}^{\prime\prime}_{3}|p)}=\left|\frac{{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s^{\prime\prime}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}^{\prime\prime}_{3})}{{\Phi}{}^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}_{s_{1}s_{2}s^{\prime}_{3}}(\bm{0},\bm{l}_{2},\bm{l}^{\prime}_{3})}\right|^{p} (139)

so that if p>1p>1 the scaling factor is higher (lower) for FCs have lower (higher) absolute value, otherwise the opposite.

E.3 Effective charges

In ionic crystals the nuclei displacement induces dipoles (proportional to the Born effective charge tensors), and this adds a dipole-dipole interaction term to the interatomic forces. This contribution, because of its long-range character (it goes as the inverse of the third power of the nuclei distances), is not suited to be Fourier interpolated and it is at the origin of the nonanalytic behavior of the dynamical matrix at Γ\Gamma, with (in general anisotropic) LO-TO splitting of the phonon frequencies at B​ZBZ center. The long-range dipole-dipole contribution to the force constants can be calculated analytically since it is fully determined by the Born effective charges (Zs∗)α​β(Z^{*}_{s})^{\alpha\beta} (effective charge tensor of atom ss) and the electronic dielectric permittivity tensor (ϵ∞)α​β(\epsilon^{\scriptscriptstyle{\infty}})^{\alpha\beta}, which can both be calculated from first principles. For a given 𝒒∈B​Z\bm{q}\in BZ, this dipole-dipole contribution is given by [92, 93]

𝚽s​t(dd)(𝒒)=𝚽^(𝒒)s​t(dd)−δs​t∑t¯𝚽^(𝒒=𝟎)s​t¯(dd)\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{st}(\bm{q})=\widehat{\bm{\Phi}}{}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{st}(\bm{q})-\delta_{st}\sum_{\overline{t}}\widehat{\bm{\Phi}}{}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{s\overline{t}}(\bm{q}=\bm{0}) (140)

with

𝚽^(𝒒)s​t(dd)=4​πΩVol∑𝑮[(𝑮+𝒒)⋅𝒁s∗]⊗[(𝑮+𝒒)⋅𝒁t∗](𝑮+𝒒)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝑮+𝒒)′e−(𝑮+𝒒)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝑮+𝒒)4​η2ei⁡(𝑮+𝒒)⋅(𝝉s−𝝉t),\widehat{\bm{\Phi}}{}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{st}(\bm{q})=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{Vol}}}}\sum_{\bm{G}}{}^{\!{}^{\prime}}\frac{\left[(\bm{G}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{Z}^{*}_{s}\right]\otimes\left[(\bm{G}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{Z}^{*}_{t}\right]}{(\bm{G}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{\epsilon}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\infty}}\cdot(\bm{G}+\bm{q})}\,e^{\textstyle-\frac{(\bm{G}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{\epsilon}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\infty}}\cdot(\bm{G}+\bm{q})}{4\eta^{2}}}\,e^{i(\bm{G}+\bm{q})\cdot(\bm{\tau}_{s}-\bm{\tau}_{t})}\,, (141)

where we have explicitly indicated only the atomic indices (i.e. we are using component-free notation for the cartesian indices), η\eta is a parameter whose value has to be large enough to allow to include only the reciprocal space terms in the Ewald sum, and ∑𝑮′\sum_{\bm{G}}^{\prime} is the sum over reciprocal lattice vectors such that 𝑮+𝒒≠𝟎\bm{G}+\bm{q}\neq\bm{0} (the sum includes as many 𝑮\bm{G}’s as it is necessary to reach the convergence for the considered η\eta) [63].

Once 𝒁s∗\bm{Z}^{*}_{s} and ϵ∞\bm{\epsilon}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\infty}} are available, the problem caused to the Fourier interpolation by the long-range dipole-dipole interaction is thus bypassed in the SSCHA code in two steps. First, from the 𝚽⁡(𝒒)\bm{\Phi}(\bm{q}) calculated on a (coarse) grid of 𝒒\bm{q} point of the Brillouin zone, the corresponding dipole-dipole terms 𝚽(dd)​(𝒒)\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}(\bm{q}) are subtracted and the resulting short range FCs is Fourier transformed to the real space. Subsequently, this real space short-range FCs, 𝚽(sr)​(𝒍)\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(sr)}}}(\bm{l}), can be Fourier transformed back to any 𝒌∈B​Z\bm{k}\in BZ and the corresponding long-range dipole-dipole analytical contribution 𝚽(dd)​(𝒌)\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}(\bm{k}) is added [63]:

𝚽⁡(𝒒) on B​Z 𝒒-grid→Subtract dipole-dipole interaction terms𝚽OPEN(​d​d)​(𝒒)+Fourier transformto real space𝚽(sr)(𝒍)→Fourier transformback to 𝒌∈B​Z+Add dipole-dipole interaction term𝚽OPEN(​d​d)​(𝒌)𝚽(𝒌)\begin{gathered}\bm{\Phi}(\bm{q})\\ \textup{ on $BZ$ $\bm{q}$-grid}\end{gathered}\xrightarrow{\begin{subarray}{c}\textup{Subtract dipole-dipole interaction terms}\\ \textup{$\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(}}dd)}(\bm{q})$}\\ $+$\\ \textup{Fourier transform}\\ \textup{to real space}\end{subarray}}\quad\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(sr)}}}(\bm{l})\quad\xrightarrow{\begin{subarray}{c}\textup{Fourier transform}\\ \textup{back to $\bm{k}\in BZ$}\\ $+$\\ \textup{Add dipole-dipole interaction term}\\ \textup{$\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(}}dd)}(\bm{k})$}\end{subarray}}\bm{\Phi}(\bm{k}) (142)

The dipole-dipole correction to the FCs given by Eqs. (140), (141) is nonanalytic at zone center and its 𝒒→𝟎\bm{q}\rightarrow\bm{0} limit depends on the direction 𝒒^=𝒒/‖𝒒‖\widehat{\bm{q}}=\bm{q}/\|\bm{q}\| along which the limit is performed:

limδ→0+𝚽(δ𝒒^)s​t(dd)=𝚽s​t(dd)(𝟎)+𝚽s​t(dd-na)(𝒒^),\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0^{+}}\bm{\Phi}{}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{st}(\delta\widehat{\bm{q}})=\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd)}}}_{st}(\bm{0})+\bm{\Phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd-na)}}}_{st}(\widehat{\bm{q}})\,, (143)

where

𝚽(𝒒^)s​t(dd-na)=4​πΩVol[𝒒^⋅𝒁s∗]⊗[𝒒^⋅𝒁t∗]𝒒^⋅ϵ∞⋅𝒒^\bm{\Phi}{}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{(dd-na)}}}_{st}(\widehat{\bm{q}})=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{\scriptscriptstyle{\text{Vol}}}}\frac{\left[\widehat{\bm{q}}\cdot\bm{Z}^{*}_{s}\right]\otimes\left[\widehat{\bm{q}}\cdot\bm{Z}^{*}_{t}\right]}{\widehat{\bm{q}}\cdot\bm{\epsilon}^{\scriptscriptstyle{\infty}}\cdot\widehat{\bm{q}}} (144)

is the nonanalytic zone-center correction term. When a phonon dispersion through Γ\Gamma is calculated, the SSCHA code includes the nonanalytic correction term in the zone center, with the direction given by the followed path [63]. When the SSCHA code calculate the spectral properties (static or dynamic), it adds the nonanalytic correction term in the zone center dynamical matrix (necessary for the integral over the BZ) from a random direction.
